clinicalPearls: Small-bowel injury from abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy, in acute and chronic forms
Acute enteritis causes nausea, cramping, diarrhoea and malabsorption during and shortly after treatment and usually settles
Chronic radiation enteropathy develops months to years later with obstruction, malabsorption, bleeding or fistulae
Fixed loops of small bowel in the pelvis (for example after surgery) are especially vulnerable
Chronic disease reflects progressive obliterative endarteritis, ischaemia and fibrosis
Management is largely supportive and nutritional; surgery for strictures or fistulae is high-risk in irradiated tissue
reference.pathophysiology: Radiation enteritis arises from ionising radiation injury to the rapidly dividing small-bowel mucosa and to the bowel vasculature. Acute injury causes mucosal cell loss, villous blunting and inflammation with malabsorption and diarrhoea, and usually recovers. Chronic radiation enteropathy results from progressive submucosal fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis, producing ischaemia, strictures, dysmotility, bacterial overgrowth, bleeding from telangiectasia and fistula formation. Risk relates to dose, technique and factors that fix bowel loops within the radiation field.
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging or contrast studies of the small bowel
Assessment of nutritional status and malabsorption
Endoscopy where accessible bowel is involved
Evaluation for bacterial overgrowth and bile acid malabsorption
redFlags: Severe malnutrition or features suggesting recurrent tumour
reference.prognosis: Acute enteritis usually resolves after treatment; chronic enteropathy is progressive and difficult to manage, with surgery carrying high complication rates in irradiated bowel.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic symptoms to recurrent cancer without considering radiation enteropathy (and vice versa)
Underestimating the surgical risk in irradiated bowel
Overlooking bacterial overgrowth and bile acid malabsorption as treatable contributors
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Acute radiation enteritis is usually self limited, resolving within two to six months, so early management is symptomatic control of diarrhea, cramping and urgency plus attention to hydration
Antidiarrheal agents, antispasmodics, and a low residue low fat diet are commonly used during treatment to reduce stool frequency and mucosal irritation
Bile acid sequestrants can be considered when bile salt malabsorption is contributing to radiotherapy induced diarrhea
Radiotherapy is not routinely interrupted for mild to moderate acute enteritis; treatment breaks are decided case by case for severe symptoms
In chronic late phase enteropathy, evaluate for and treat bacterial overgrowth, especially when strictures or enterocolic fistulas are present
Distinguish radiation induced pancolitis from true inflammatory bowel disease when a colitis picture develops, since management differs
For late radiation proctitis, Grade 2 rectal bleeding can be treated with steroid suppositories, sitz baths, and increased dietary fiber
Avoid deep rectal biopsies and cauterization procedures unless absolutely necessary due to increased risk of mucosal trauma and fistula formation
For proctitis not responding to conservative measures, argon beam plasma laser coagulation can reduce rectal bleeding episodes, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy may also help
Reserve surgery for structural complications such as obstruction, stricture, or fistula, recognizing that operating on irradiated bowel carries a high complication rate

When radiation enteritis contributes to malignant bowel obstruction, use standard supportive measures including nasogastric decompression, intravenous hydration, and antisecretory agents, steroids or scopolamine, plus analgesics and antiemetics

Consider home parenteral nutrition only in patients with good performance status, caretaker support, and an expected survival long enough to justify it, with quality of life as the primary consideration in the palliative setting
Monitor nutritional status, weight, and signs of malabsorption or bacterial overgrowth longitudinally in chronic radiation enteropathy

Refer to gastroenterology, colorectal surgery, or nutrition and palliative care when conservative measures fail, when obstruction, stricture or fistula develops, or when parenteral nutrition is being considered
